doc.title: Laurence Juber interviewed by Monk Rowe, Glasgow, Scotland, July 27, 2016 [interview 1 of 2]

title: Wings audition, union payments, royalties and mentor David Katz
summary: He describes the audition, AFM union checks, residuals and performance royalties, and fixer David Katz who got him into 'The Spy Who Loved Me'.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: I borrowed some Wings LPs from my brother. And it turned out that what we played was some Chuck Berry tunes and some reggae grooves and they offered me the gig. But when I got to L.A. it was a very different world, because the union, the AF of M was much more involved than the English musicians’ union. So all of a sudden I find myself — you know I did some jingle sessions in New York for Lincoln Mercury and then all of a sudden I’m getting all these checks. Whereas in England I’d go to an 8 AM jingle and you’d get paid for the session and that’s the end of it. I’m starting to get checks from Local 802 in New York, and then when I moved to L.A., Local 47, and I’m getting into doing movie sessions. And I played on — there was one piece of original music on The Big Chill where one of the characters has a T.V. show and we recorded a theme for that T.V. show. And the next July I get a check from the secondary payments fund for many thousands of dollars, because there were only a small group of musicians who played on the score. And that’s when I discovered that. And then when I started getting into composing and I did the Brady Bunch Christmas movie, “A Very Brady Christmas” and all of a sudden I get this package in the mail and I qualified for health insurance. So it was a different — it was a more involved business model. And now, since Sound Exchange, I get performance royalties for my airplay on Pandora or Sirius, for my own stuff, but also the secondary markets fund from SAG AFTRA now have a performance fund, PPL which is the U.K. one which picks up the neighboring rights. That’s where I see more money from the Wings records that I played on for example. And it was only later that I started learning about ASCAP and BMI and being able to pick up kind of the writer side of it. So that kind of expanded my vision of where the revenue streams were. But to begin with it was just write out a little invoice, send it to the contractor or “fixer” as we call them in England. A man named David Katz was the one who got me started. © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

He’d seen me on television with the National Youth Jazz Orchestra and called me up the next day and said — he called everybody darling. He said, “Darling, I’ve got some sessions for you.” And he gave me the dates. I said, “David, I hate to say this, but those are my final exams for my bachelor of music degree.” And I just couldn’t — you know I’d been studying for three years, I wasn’t going to skip the finals. And I didn’t think I’d hear from him again, but as it turned out he called a couple of weeks later. And he became my kind of studio mentor. And eventually he got me into the session for “The Spy Who Loved Me” and I got to play the James Bond theme, which, how cool is that?
